name: Guyana Business Plan Knowledge Pack
purpose: Offline retrieval pack for Guyana-focused business-plan generation. Designed to be replaced and expanded in future app versions.

chunks.title: Guyana market snapshot
chunks.text:
Guyana uses the Guyana dollar (GYD). The 2022 national population and housing census counted 878,674 people on census night. The Bureau of Statistics reported that 87.16% of the preliminary census population lived in coastal regions. For planning, location matters: Region 4 (Demerara-Mahaica) is the most densely populated region, while interior regions are much more sparsely populated. The ten administrative regions are Barima-Waini; Pomeroon-Supenaam; Essequibo Islands-West Demerara; Demerara-Mahaica; Mahaica-Berbice; East Berbice-Corentyne; Cuyuni-Mazaruni; Potaro-Siparuni; Upper Takutu-Upper Essequibo; and Upper Demerara-Berbice.

In August 2026, the Georgetown CPI was 153.33, with 12-month point-to-point inflation of 3.6% and 12-month average inflation of 3.5%. Use these as a dated macroeconomic reference only, not as an automatic price escalator. A business plan should ask the user for current local supplier prices and wage quotes wherever possible.

chunks.title: Business name registration
chunks.text:
A sole trader or partnership trading under a business name in Guyana generally registers that name with the Deeds and Commercial Registries Authority (DCRA). Current Government/DCRA information lists a new business-name application fee of GYD 5,000, renewal of GYD 2,500, Statement of Change of GYD 2,000, and a current processing time of about 7 working days. Typical required items include the completed application, identity document, TIN certificate and fee. The registration must be renewed when due, changes should be filed, and discontinuance should be notified when the business stops trading.

Do not tell a user that a business-name registration creates a separate legal company. A sole trader remains legally distinct from an incorporated company structure.

chunks.title: Company incorporation
chunks.text: A company is incorporated under the Companies Act through the DCRA. Current official guidance lists Articles of Incorporation, director/secretary notices and consents, registered-office notice, declaration of compliance, name search/reservation, and identity documents among the required items. The published basic fees are GYD 60,000 prescribed incorporation fee, GYD 3,200 for notices and GYD 350 mandatory copy, totalling GYD 63,550. The stated processing time is about 3 working days once a complete application is accepted. Companies have continuing obligations such as annual returns, financial statements, beneficial-ownership declarations, and notifications of changes.

chunks.title: TIN and tax registration
chunks.text: Businesses need a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) relationship with the Guyana Revenue Authority. GRA guidance for an individual business notes that a sole trader can use the individual's TIN to register for a Business TIN rather than obtaining a company TIN. Supporting information can include identity, proof of address, business registration, and projected financial statements. The current published fee for a new TIN certificate is GYD 1,000. Treat the TIN as a compliance prerequisite in a plan whenever the business will transact formally, hire, seek SBB support, import, or file taxes.

chunks.title: VAT rules for planning
chunks.text:
The standard VAT rate in Guyana is 14% unless a supply is exempt or zero-rated. Mandatory VAT registration generally applies when taxable activity equals or exceeds GYD 15,000,000 over a 12-month period, exceeds that amount in less than 12 months, or is expected to exceed it during the next 12 months. Businesses below the threshold may apply for voluntary registration subject to GRA criteria. Only a VAT-registered person should charge VAT. VAT-registered businesses must issue appropriate tax invoices for taxable supplies.

When building projections, never add 14% VAT blindly. First classify the product/service as standard-rated, zero-rated, exempt or out of scope. If uncertain, mark the VAT treatment as 'verify with GRA'.

chunks.title: Individual and self-employed income tax — 2026
chunks.text: For 2026, the annual personal deduction is GYD 1,680,000 or one-third of qualifying income from all sources, whichever is greater. Chargeable income up to GYD 3,360,000 is taxed at 25%; chargeable income above that ceiling is taxed at 35%. The GRA also publishes deductions/allowances for NIS, qualifying medical/life insurance, children under 18, second-job income and overtime. For business-plan projections, calculate business profit first; owner tax should then be estimated separately and labelled as an estimate rather than treated as an operating expense unless the accounting treatment calls for it.

chunks.title: Corporation tax
chunks.text: GRA currently publishes corporation-tax rates of 45% of chargeable profits for telephone companies, 40% for commercial companies other than telephone companies, and 25% for other companies. A company conducting both commercial and non-commercial activities can face dual rates. GRA also states that where corporation tax paid by a commercial company is less than 2% of turnover, a 2% turnover tax can apply. The legal classification of 'commercial' versus other activity matters, so a plan should flag the rate for confirmation with GRA or a tax professional rather than assuming every incorporated business is automatically taxed at 40%.

chunks.title: Key tax filing dates
chunks.text: Individual income-tax and corporation-tax returns are generally due by April 30 for the relevant year of assessment, subject to next-business-day treatment where applicable. GRA publishes corporate advance-tax due dates of March 15, June 15, September 15 and December 15. A business plan should include a compliance calendar and cash reserve for tax payments rather than assuming taxes are paid only once at year-end.

chunks.title: National Insurance Scheme (NIS)
chunks.text: For employed contributors, total NIS contributions are 14% of insurable earnings: 5.6% deducted from the employee and 8.4% paid by the employer. The published insurable-earnings ceiling is GYD 280,000 per month or GYD 64,615 per week. Self-employed persons contribute 12.5% of declared income. Payroll projections should include the employer's 8.4% NIS cost up to the applicable ceiling; the employee contribution is a payroll deduction rather than an additional employer cost.

chunks.title: Wages, hours, overtime and leave
chunks.text:
The Ministry of Labour's currently published national minimum wage is GYD 347 hourly, GYD 2,776 daily, GYD 13,880 weekly and GYD 60,147 monthly, effective from 1 July 2022. The Ministry's overtime/leave guidance states a normal work week of 40 hours over no more than 5 days, normally 8 hours per day. Work beyond normal hours generally attracts at least 1.5 times the normal rate; special rules can apply to factories and public holidays. Minimum paid leave for weekly, fortnightly or monthly workers is one day for each completed month of employment; daily/hourly formulas differ.

Because wage orders can change, tag this fact as time-sensitive and verify before a plan is submitted to a lender or used for hiring.
chunks.source: Ministry of Labour and Manpower Planning

chunks.title: Small Business Bureau definition
chunks.text: The Small Business Bureau (SBB) states that a small business must satisfy all three limits: no more than 25 employees, gross annual revenue no more than GYD 60 million, and total business assets no more than GYD 20 million. When generating a plan for an SBB applicant, explicitly test all three criteria and report whether the supplied figures appear to fit the SBB definition.

chunks.title: SBB loan support and documents
chunks.text: SBB's Credit Guarantee Programme currently supports small-business development loans up to GYD 30 million through participating financial institutions. SBB publishes collateral coverage of up to 40% for first-time borrowers and up to 70% for repeat borrowers; its site advertises a 6% interest rate. Published eligibility/documentation includes SBB registration, business registration, ID, TIN, quotations or estimates for items to be financed, collateral information, GRA/NIS compliance, credit information, and a complete business plan for a startup or a business established less than 12 months. Treat lender approval as separate from SBB eligibility.

chunks.title: Government procurement opportunity
chunks.text: The Small Business Procurement Programme is designed to facilitate 20% of Government procurement of goods, services and works from small businesses. SBB lists documents such as the procurement form, ID, TIN certificate, GRA compliance, NIS documentation and business registration. For a plan targeting government clients, include procurement readiness: formal registration, tax/NIS compliance, tender capacity, delivery standards, cash-flow needs while awaiting payment, and record keeping.

chunks.title: GO-Invest and incentives
chunks.text: GO-Invest facilitates local and foreign investment, provides sector information, and helps qualifying projects pursue fiscal incentives and investment agreements. GRA explains that investment agreements can support exemptions or zero-rating where a project and listed items qualify and the relevant approvals are obtained. Incentives are not automatic. A business plan should describe potential concessions as 'subject to eligibility and approval' and never reduce startup costs by an incentive unless the user confirms an approved concession or investment agreement.

chunks.title: Environmental authorization
chunks.text: Projects with potential environmental impacts—such as construction, industrial operations or resource extraction—may require Environmental Authorization from the EPA. An authorization may take the form of an environmental, construction, operating or prescribed-process permit depending on the project. Plans for manufacturing, mining, large agriculture, waste handling, energy, major construction or other potentially impactful activities should include an EPA screening/authorization checkpoint before operations begin.

chunks.title: Food businesses and food handlers
chunks.text: Food businesses can face multiple requirements. The Guyana Food Safety Authority licenses food business operators, issues food-handler and street-food permits and inspects food premises. Food handlers need appropriate training/certification, and medical requirements may also apply. The Government Analyst Food and Drug Department (GA-FDD) inspects and licenses manufacturers/importers of regulated foods and publishes specific service fees. A restaurant, caterer, processor, beverage maker or food importer should have a compliance workstream rather than a generic 'business licence' line.
chunks.source: Government of Guyana Portal / Guyana Food Safety Authority

chunks.title: Selected GA-FDD fees
chunks.text: GA-FDD's published Inspectorate price list includes: application/renewal of a licence to manufacture food — GYD 5,000; permit to manufacture/repackage foods — GYD 1,500; permit to import foods — GYD 20,000; food-handler permit processing — GYD 500; and certificate of free sale — GYD 5,000 per certificate. These are service-specific and should not be treated as a complete licensing budget. Verify current fees and which authority has jurisdiction before finalizing the plan.
chunks.source: Government Analyst Food and Drug Department

chunks.title: Fire safety and LPG/petroleum
chunks.text: Certain business premises require Guyana Fire Service certification, including examples such as hotels, bars, liquor restaurants, sawmills, lumber yards, mechanical workshops and spare-parts stores. Fire-safety approval can involve building-plan/CH&PA or local-authority documentation and inspection. Businesses storing petroleum or LPG cylinders may need a separate storage licence and fire-safety inspection. Include fire-safety equipment, inspection and approval in the startup checklist where the premises or materials warrant it.
chunks.source: Government of Guyana Portal / Guyana Fire Service

chunks.title: Standards and quality systems
chunks.text: The Guyana National Bureau of Standards supports standards, metrology and business competitiveness. Depending on sector, a business may benefit from or need product/measurement compliance, calibration or recognised quality systems. For export, manufacturing, laboratories, construction materials or food production, the plan should ask whether GNBS standards, calibration or certification requirements apply and budget for testing/quality assurance where relevant.

chunks.title: Recommended Guyana business-plan structure
chunks.text:
Generate plans in this order: 1) cover and business identity; 2) executive summary; 3) problem/opportunity; 4) product/service and value proposition; 5) location and Guyana market context; 6) target customers; 7) competitor/alternative analysis; 8) marketing and sales; 9) operations and suppliers; 10) ownership/management and staffing; 11) registration, tax, NIS, permits and compliance; 12) startup budget and funding request; 13) pricing and unit economics; 14) 12-month sales and cash-flow forecast; 15) profit-and-loss summary; 16) break-even; 17) risks and mitigations; 18) implementation timeline; 19) funding use and repayment capacity if debt-funded; 20) assumptions and source notes.

For SBB or lender use, attach quotations/estimates and clearly distinguish confirmed amounts from assumptions.

chunks.title: Assumption discipline
chunks.text: The local model must not invent current rent, wages above statutory minimum, supplier prices, loan interest rates, customs duties, electricity bills, competitor prices or sales volumes. When the user has not supplied a figure, use one of three states: CONFIRMED (user/document supplied), ESTIMATE (explicit planning assumption), or VERIFY (requires current external confirmation). Every financial table should carry an assumptions block. If a number materially drives profitability, ask the user for it before finalizing the plan whenever possible.

chunks.title: Offline market sizing methods
chunks.text: Without live search, size the market from user-provided or bundled data using transparent methods. Bottom-up: number of reachable customers × purchase frequency × average spend. Capacity-based: maximum jobs/units/rooms × realistic utilization × price. Location-based: households/businesses in the stated catchment × estimated penetration × spend. Contract-based: number of signed/probable contracts × value. Always show the formula and separate Total Addressable Market, Serviceable Available Market and realistic first-year target. Do not derive a market-share percentage from national population when the business serves only a village, region or niche.

chunks.title: Pricing framework
chunks.text: Evaluate pricing from three angles: cost floor, competitor/customer reference supplied by the user, and value delivered. Calculate unit variable cost, contribution per unit, contribution margin percentage and required sales volume. For services, include labour hours, transport, consumables and rework. For retail, include landed purchase cost, shrinkage and payment charges. For food, include yield/waste and packaging. Never recommend a price solely by applying a generic markup; show how the proposed price covers costs and fits the target customer's willingness to pay.

chunks.title: Cash-flow planning
chunks.text: A profitable business can still fail from cash shortage. Build monthly cash flow with opening cash, cash sales, collections from credit sales, owner capital/loan inflows, operating payments, inventory purchases, payroll including employer NIS, rent/utilities, tax/VAT payments where applicable, debt service and capital purchases. Track closing cash and identify the lowest cash month. Funding need should cover startup capital plus the maximum projected cash deficit, not just equipment purchases.

chunks.title: Break-even analysis
chunks.text: Break-even units = monthly fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit, where contribution per unit = selling price − variable cost per unit. Break-even revenue = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin ratio. For mixed products, use a weighted-average contribution margin based on the expected sales mix. If contribution is zero or negative, stop and flag the pricing/cost structure rather than producing a meaningless break-even figure.

chunks.title: Scenario analysis
chunks.text: Produce at least three scenarios when the plan depends on uncertain demand: conservative, base and upside. Change only key drivers such as units sold, occupancy, average order value, raw-material cost or collection delay. Do not arbitrarily change every line. Report revenue, gross profit, operating profit, closing cash and break-even timing for each scenario. The base case should be plausible, not automatically the midpoint.

chunks.title: Agriculture & Farming
chunks.text:
Use this playbook when the user's primary sector is Agriculture & Farming.
Revenue drivers: crop/livestock output, acreage, yield, cycles, farm-gate price.
Cost drivers: seed/stock, feed/fertiliser, labour, irrigation, fuel, transport, loss/spoilage.
Compliance questions: land tenure, drainage/irrigation, biosecurity, EPA where relevant, food safety for processed output.
Key performance indicators: yield per acre/animal, mortality/loss rate, cost per kg/unit, gross margin, harvest cycle.
Common risks to test: weather/flooding, pests/disease, input price volatility, market access.

Ask for location, startup stage, available capital, ownership, customer type, price assumptions, capacity, staffing, supplier information and financing method. Build projections from the user's operating capacity and prices rather than generic industry averages.

chunks.title: Import/export planning
chunks.text: For an import-dependent business, calculate landed cost as supplier price plus international freight, insurance if applicable, customs duties/taxes that actually apply, local port/broker/transport costs, and expected loss/damage. Do not assume duty-free treatment. Some investments can qualify for concessions through GO-Invest/GRA, but only after eligibility and approval. For food imports, GA-FDD permits can apply; other regulated goods may need licences, standards or agency approvals. For export plans, include packaging/label standards, transport, documentation, payment terms and destination-market requirements.

chunks.title: Record keeping and controls
chunks.text: Recommend basic controls appropriate to a small Guyanese business: separate business cash/bank/MMG activity from personal spending; numbered invoices/receipts; daily sales summary; purchase and expense records; inventory count where applicable; payroll and NIS records; tax/VAT files; supplier/customer balances; monthly bank reconciliation; and monthly profit/cash-flow review. For cash-heavy businesses, include till reconciliation and deposit controls. For mobile-money receipts, reconcile wallet transactions to invoices and settlement records.
